attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, restating his earlier argument as his current view.

semantics.note: Keeps the 'most AI companies' scope and the liquidity framing. 'Really is no' is firm, not hedged. The 'exit/liquidity path' wording is a fair paraphrase.

contract.note: The plain reading (most venture-backed AI companies lack a feasible investor liquidity route) is ordinary and fair. The population, the meaning of 'most', and the window are evaluator choices, so interpretation drives the result.

evidence.note: HKEX filing confirms MiniMax listed Jan 9, 2026, inside the window. It is one company and says nothing about most AI companies. Lockups limit immediate liquidity.

Crunchbase Q1 2026 data: weak US IPOs, Chinese AI lab listings, strong startup M&A. Covers all sectors and the full quarter, with no AI-company denominator, so it cannot show what fraction had feasible routes.

reviews.rationale: Completed exits (MiniMax, Z.ai, active M&A) undercut an absolute no-exit reading. But the claim is about most AI companies, and the packet sets no population or share with or without feasible liquidity routes. The evidence neither meets the support condition nor the contradiction condition.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: A faithful paraphrase. The claim is evaluative but asserts something factual: that the industry's economics are brittle and that this has been obscured.

contract.note: The reading (disclosures materially obscured weak economics, with no intent required) is ordinary and fair. Industry breadth, the degree of brittleness, and the Q4 2025 window are evaluator-supplied.

evidence.note: FMTI Dec 2025 finds labs rarely disclose model-building costs. This partly supports the disclosure-gap half only. It does not show brittleness or industry-wide obscuring of fragility.
CoreWeave's FY2025 10-K, filed before the post, openly discloses losses and profitability risk. It cuts against blanket concealment but covers one firm only.

reviews.rationale: The evidence shows some cost-disclosure gaps (e3) and some candid risk disclosure (e4). Nothing representative compares disclosures with underlying fragility across the industry, so neither the support nor the contradiction condition is met.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Keeps 'this entire time' and 'massively'. Context points to OpenAI and Anthropic subscriptions.

contract.note: Reading subsidy as receipts below actual delivery cost is ordinary and fair. But Zitron's examples use API-priced value, so choosing the cost basis likely decides the result. The contract's 'false' flag understates this.

evidence.note: Altman's Jan 2025 admission of losses on ChatGPT Pro. A company statement about one product at one time, with no cost breakdown. Too narrow for a persistent, cross-lab claim.

Anthropic S-1 (filed before the cutoff): 2025 revenue exceeds cost of revenue company-wide. Aggregate figures that include API revenue, and free-tier compute is booked in S&M. Does not isolate subscription margins.

reviews.rationale: Neither lab has a subscription-level series of revenue and delivery costs in the packet. One OpenAI product admission and Anthropic's positive aggregate gross margin point in different directions and do not settle a persistent, massive subsidy across products and labs.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Keeps both plan ratios. 'Before generous usage' is reflected by leaving bonus usage out. 'After repricing' fairly renders 'even with this pricing'.

contract.note: In context Zitron describes included tokens matching or exceeding the fee, so reading 'gives away' as excess included API-priced value is ordinary and fair. Treating 16 cents as an approximation of 16⅔ is reasonable.

evidence.note: Cursor staff reply, Mar 27, 2026: Pro+ $60 includes $70 of usage and Ultra $200 includes $400. That gives about 16.7¢ and $1 excess per dollar. A company disclosure, but the authoritative source for its own plan terms.

reviews.rationale: Cursor's March 2026 plan terms give $10 extra on $60 (about 16.7¢ per dollar, roughly the stated 16¢) and $200 extra on $200 (exactly $1 per dollar). This supports the included-value reading. It does not establish Cursor's actual losses.
